sections.heading: Strongly-typed CSS utility classes using C# (supports Blazor, Razor Pages and MVC)
sections.text: FluentCss lets you compose Tailwind-inspired utility classes with a type-safe, chainable API. You write C#, the library generates the class names and the CSS. Get started Browse utilities Generated entirely from C#
sections.code: Generated entirely from C#

sections.heading: Type-safe
sections.text: Every utility is a method. Rename, refactor and navigate styles with the same tooling you already use for C#.

sections.heading: Tailwind palette
sections.text: 22 color families with 11 shades each (50 to 950), plus black and white, ready to use.

sections.heading: States and responsive
sections.text: Compose hover, focus and active states, then layer responsive min/md and max/md variants on top.

sections.heading: Dark mode built in
sections.text: Use the Dark builder for theme-aware styles, or Theme() for any custom theme name.

sections.heading: Automatic CSS
sections.text: Classes are deduplicated in a registry that emits the final CSS for you.

sections.heading: Blazor ready
sections.text: Drop the CssStyles component into your layout and the stylesheet updates as you build.

sections.heading: Installation
sections.text: Pick the package for your hosting model, wire FluentCss up once and start composing styles.

sections.heading: Choose a package
sections.text: There is one integration package per hosting model. Install the one that matches your app. You never install yourself. Package Hosting model What it gives you Blazor The component and the preflight stylesheet. Use it for Blazor static SSR, Blazor Server, Blazor WebAssembly (standalone) and Blazor Web Apps using the Interactive Server, Interactive WebAssembly or Auto render mode. ASP.NET Core MVC and Razor Pages The tag helper, the stylesheet middleware and the preflight stylesheet. FluentCss.Core comes with them Both integration packages depend on and bring it in automatically. That is where the builder, the registry and every utility live, and it is a transitive dependency: do not add it to your project on its own.
sections.code: FluentCss.Core FluentCss.Blazor CssStyles FluentCss.MvcRazor <fluent-css /> FluentCss.Core

sections.heading: Blazor
sections.text: Add the Blazor package: For the shortest syntax add the following to your . Importing the static builder means you can start a chain with or directly. Drop the component into your layout. It renders a block with every class registered while the page is built. Optionally include the Tailwind preflight reset to normalize browser defaults such as margins, borders and fonts:
sections.code: dotnet add package FluentCss.Blazor _Imports.razor Css Dark @using static FluentCss.Core.FluentCssBuilder @using FluentCss.Core CssStyles <style> <!-- MainLayout.razor or App.razor --> ... <head> ... <!-- Add Tailwind CSS preflight, optional but strongly recommended --> <link rel="stylesheet" href="_content/FluentCss.Blazor/preflight.css" /> <FluentCss.Blazor.CssStyles /> ... </head> <body>...</body>

sections.heading: Interactive rendering
sections.text: is more than a snapshot of the classes seen so far: it subscribes to the class registry and re-renders its block whenever a new class is registered. A component that renders later on the client - a dialog, a tab or anything that only appears after a click - is therefore styled as soon as it renders, with no page reload. For that to work has to live inside the interactive render boundary. In a Blazor Web App that means the layout, or anything else under , rather than the statically rendered head: Registration follows the process Classes are registered in the process that renders the component. A prerender fills the server registry; interactive WebAssembly fills one inside the browser; an interactive server circuit runs in the server process and shares its registry with the prerender. Whichever runtime is active owns a instance and re-emits the stylesheet when that runtime registers new classes. The Interactive Server, Interactive WebAssembly and Auto render modes are all supported.
sections.code: CssStyles <style> CssStyles <Routes> App.razor <!-- App.razor: the render mode decides where interactivity runs --> <Routes @rendermode="InteractiveWebAssembly" /> <!-- MainLayout.razor: CssStyles is part of the interactive tree --> @inherits LayoutComponentBase <FluentCss.Blazor.CssStyles /> <main>@Body</main> CssStyles

sections.heading: MVC and Razor Pages
sections.text: Add the MVC/Razor Pages package: Register the middleware in . It serves the current hash at and the stylesheet at , with gzip and an ETag. Razor Pages apps map their pages instead with ; the middleware and the tag helper are identical for both models. Register the tag helper and the namespaces in (or ): Finally add the tag helper and the preflight stylesheet to your layout. The tag helper renders the stylesheet and a small script that keeps it in sync after client-side DOM changes, such as a partial view loaded over AJAX. No need to add hash or timestamp The tag helper resolves the current hash when the layout renders, but classes can still be registered after that point. The injected script re-reads on load and watches the document for later changes, swapping the stylesheet when it changes.
sections.code: dotnet add package FluentCss.MvcRazor Program.cs /fluentcss/hash /fluentcss/{hash}.css var app = builder.Build(); app.UseRouting(); app.UseFluentCssMvcRazor(); // serve /fluentcss/hash and /fluentcss/{hash}.css app.UseAuthorization(); app.MapStaticAssets(); app.MapControllerRoute("default", "{controller=Home}/{action=Index}/{id?}"); app.MapRazorPages() _ViewImports.cshtml Pages/_ViewImports.cshtml @using static FluentCss.Core.FluentCssBuilder @using FluentCss.Core @addTagHelper *, FluentCss.MvcRazor <link> <head> ... <link rel="stylesheet" href="/_content/FluentCss.MvcRazor/preflight.css" /> <fluent-css /> </head> /fluentcss/hash

sections.heading: Any other .NET project
sections.text: Outside of Blazor and MVC/Razor Pages there is no integration package, so add the core library directly: You can then build classes and read the generated CSS from any .NET application. returns the space separated class names for your attribute, while gives you the stylesheet.
sections.code: dotnet add package FluentCss.Core ToString() class ClassRegistry.DefaultRegistry.Css using FluentCss.Core; var classes = FluentCssBuilder.Css .Background(Color.Emerald500) .Color(Color.White) .Px(6) .Py(3) .RoundedMd(); // "bg-emerald-500 text-white px-6 py-3 rounded-md" string classAttr = classes.ToString(); // The complete, deduplicated stylesheet string css = ClassRegistry.DefaultRegistry.Css;

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: FluentCss turns method calls into utility classes, collects them in a registry and emits a single stylesheet.

sections.heading: The pipeline
sections.text: 1. You call a fluent method such as . 2. A is created: a CSS property, a value and a generated class name. 3. The class is added to a . Duplicates are ignored. 4. The registry appends the CSS rule and invalidates its cached output. 5. on the builder returns the class names for your markup.
sections.code: .Background(Color.Red500) UtilityClass ClassRegistry ToString()

sections.heading: A utility class
sections.text: Every call produces one utility. The builder keeps the class names in order, so the string returned by matches the order in which you composed it.
sections.code: ToString() var button = FluentCssBuilder.Css .Background(Color.Blue500) .Color(Color.White) .Px(6) .Py(3) .RoundedMd(); string classes = button.ToString(); // bg-blue-500 text-white px-6 py-3 rounded-md

sections.heading: Class name format
sections.text: A generated class name is assembled from the active variants, in this order: Utility Generated CSS The same information drives the selector. Variant prefixes are escaped with a backslash so the colon can appear inside a CSS class name.
sections.code: [media]:[theme]:[pseudo]:utility bg-red-500 no variant hover:bg-red-600 pseudo state theme-dark:text-white theme (dark mode) min-md:flex media query theme-dark:hover:bg-slate-700 theme and pseudo min-md:theme-dark:focus:opacity-0 media, theme and pseudo .bg-blue-500 { background-color: oklch(0.623 0.214 259.815) } .text-white { color: #fff } .px-6 { padding-inline: 1.5rem } .py-3 { padding-block: 0.75rem } .rounded-md { border-radius: 0.375rem } /* variants are escaped and scoped */ .hover\:bg-blue-600:hover { background-color: oklch(0.546 0.245 262.881) } @media (width > 48rem) { .min-md\:flex { display: flex } } .theme-dark .theme-dark\:text-white { color: #fff }

sections.heading: The registry
sections.text: is a process wide collection. Because a utility is only added once, calling the same method from several components produces a single CSS rule. The registry also exposes the final output:
sections.code: ClassRegistry.DefaultRegistry // Add through the builder (recommended) FluentCssBuilder.Css.Background(Color.Red500); // Read the generated stylesheet string css = ClassRegistry.DefaultRegistry.Css; // UTF-8 bytes, handy for writing a file or streaming byte[] bytes = ClassRegistry.DefaultRegistry.CssUtf8;

sections.heading: Performance
sections.text: FluentCss is designed so the common case is cheap. This page explains where the cost actually lives and the few habits that keep a large app fast.

sections.heading: Where the cost is
sections.text: There are three distinct costs, and they behave very differently: 1. Building the class string. Every time a chain such as is evaluated, the builder creates a per utility, builds each class name, collects them and joins the result. This runs on every render where the expression appears. 2. Adding to the registry. Each utility is looked up in . If it is already known, the call is a dictionary lookup and nothing else happens. 3. Generating the stylesheet. Only a new class appends a rule and invalidates the cached string. Once every class is known, the stylesheet is never rebuilt again. The short version The registry and the generated CSS settle down after warm-up. The only cost that keeps repeating on every render is building the class strings.
sections.code: Css.Px(4).Py(2) UtilityClass ClassRegistry.DefaultRegistry Css

sections.heading: Precompute class strings
sections.text: Define styles once in a field or get-only property and use the resulting string in markup. The builder then runs once per process, and every render becomes a field read. This is the single most valuable habit. It keeps the per-utility object, string and list allocations, plus the registry lookup, out of the render path entirely. This documentation is built the same way: all of the class strings you see here are precomputed once.
sections.code: static public static class Styles { public static string Button { get; } = $"{Css.Px(6).Py(3) .Background(Color.Blue600) .Color(Color.White) .FontBold() .Hover(h => h.Background(Color.Blue700))}"; } // Rendered as many times as you like, the builder only ran once. <button class="@Styles.Button">Save</button>

sections.heading: Select between precomputed variants
sections.text: When a style depends on state, build each variant once and choose between them. Do not rebuild the chain inside the selection.
sections.code: private static readonly string NavLink = $"{Css.Px(3).Py(2).RoundedMd() .Color(Color.Slate600) .Hover(h => h.Background(Color.Slate100))}"; private static readonly string NavLinkActive = $"{Css.Px(3).Py(2).RoundedMd() .FontBold() .Background(Color.Blue100) .Color(Color.Blue700)}"; // Only the selection runs per render. private string ClassFor(string href) => IsActive(href) ? NavLinkActive : NavLink;

sections.heading: Keep builders out of loops
sections.text: A chain written inside an or loop is evaluated for every iteration. When the set of variants is modest, build the strings once (for example into a array) and index into them.
sections.code:
@foreach @for static readonly private static readonly string[] Swatches = [.. Shades.Select(c => $"{Css.H(8).Grow()} {Css.Background(c)}")]; // ... @for (var i = 0; i < Shades.Length; i++) {
}

sections.heading: Keep the set of classes bounded
sections.text: The registry is process wide and never evicts entries. Every distinct class is retained for the life of the process and, the first time it is seen, triggers a full rebuild of the stylesheet. Utilities that accept arbitrary integers ( , , , , ...) can therefore grow memory and CPU without bound when the values come from user input or computed layout. Keep values on a scale Prefer the fixed Tailwind scale over arbitrary values. Treat any utility value derived from user input as a potential memory leak: the class, its CSS rule and its contribution to the stylesheet are never released.
sections.code: P(n) W(n) Z(n) Opacity(n)

sections.heading: What you do not need to worry about
sections.text: • Calling the same utility many times. A repeated is a dictionary lookup. Do not cache or batch registrations by hand. • The one-time startup burst. The first page that introduces many new classes pays for a stylesheet rebuild per new class, but only once per process and only for pages that have not been seen before. • A handful of inline chains outside loops. A few builder calls per component are negligible next to Blazor's own rendering work.
sections.code: Add

sections.heading: Order of magnitude
sections.text: For reference, on a desktop-class CPU registering 500 utilities takes on the order of a few tens of microseconds when the classes are new, and roughly half that when they are already known. Per utility that is well under a microsecond. The numbers only start to matter when a builder runs on every render of every row of a large list, which is exactly what precomputing avoids.

sections.heading: Checklist
sections.text: ✓ Precompute class strings as members. ✓ Choose between precomputed variants instead of rebuilding. ✓ Move builder chains out of and loops. ✓ Keep utility values on a bounded scale.

sections.heading: Styling with utility classes
sections.text: A utility class maps one small piece of CSS. Combine them to build any design without leaving C#.

sections.heading: Compose instead of names
sections.text: A utility does one thing: set a background, a padding, a display mode, and so on. Instead of inventing a class name for every component, you chain a handful of utilities together. Card title A few chained utilities.

sections.heading: Entry points
sections.text: Every chain starts with one of three roots. The root decides the variant prefix applied to the whole chain. Utility Generated CSS
sections.code: Css no prefix, theme-neutral styles Dark theme-dark: prefix, applies inside the dark theme Theme("halloween") theme-halloween: prefix, any custom theme

sections.heading: Chaining
sections.text: Utility methods return the builder, so calls can be chained or spread over several statements. Each call registers a class immediately.
sections.code: // One chain, many utilities var card = FluentCssBuilder.Css .P(6) .RoundedLg() .Background(Color.White) .ShadowMd(); // Or spread over statements; they register in order card = card.Color(Color.Slate900); card = card.Hover(h => h.ShadowLg());

sections.heading: Using the result in Razor
sections.text: On a plain HTML element you can call the builder inline. FluentCss returns an object whose is the class attribute value. Styled inline on an HTML element. Blazor components need a variable Blazor does not allow complex C# expressions in the attributes of a component. The inline chain below will not compile. Precompute the class string and pass a simple variable instead. A common pattern is to keep reusable class strings in a static class. Because the builder works anywhere, the strings can be cached and shared. Inside a component the result can also be interpolated with other expressions:
sections.code:
ToString()

Styled inline on an HTML element.

@* Does not compile on a component. *@ Home @* Precompute the class string first. *@ Home @code { private static string NavLinkClass = Css.Background(Color.Blue500).Color(Color.White).ToString()!; } using FluentCss.Core; using static FluentCss.Core.FluentCssBuilder; public static class MyStyles { public static string PrimaryButton { get; } = Css.InlineBlock().Px(6).Py(3).RoundedMd().FontBold() .Background(Color.Blue600).Color(Color.White) .Hover(h => h.Background(Color.Blue700)) .Focus(f => f.Ring(3, Color.Blue300).OutlineHidden()) .ToString()!; } Home @* Mix literals, static styles and inline chains *@ Mixed

sections.heading: Deduplication
sections.text: Registering the same utility twice only emits one CSS rule. The registry compares classes by their generated name, so the more often a utility is used the more the stylesheet is reused.
sections.code: var a = new ClassRegistry(); a.Add(new UtilityClass("p-4", "padding", "1rem")); a.Add(new UtilityClass("p-4", "padding", "1rem")); // ignored // a.Css contains exactly one .p-4 rule

sections.heading: Hover, focus and other states
sections.text: Pseudo-classes are just another fluent call. Wrap the styles you want and FluentCss prefixes the class names.

sections.heading: Built-in states
sections.text: Three helpers cover the common interactions. Pass an action that receives a and style the element as usual. Utility Generated CSS Blue button Green button
sections.code: IOnlyStyleBuilder Hover(h => ...) hover: prefix, :hover selector Focus(f => ...) focus: prefix, :focus selector Active(a => ...) active: prefix, :active selector Pseudo("first-child", x => ...) first-child: prefix with a matching selector <button class="@Css.Px(6).Py(3).RoundedMd().FontBold().CursorPointer() @Css.Background(Color.Blue500).Color(Color.White) @Css.Hover(h => h.Background(Color.Blue600)) @Css.Active(a => a.Background(Color.Blue700)) @Css.Focus(f => f.Ring(3, Color.Blue300).OutlineHidden())"> Blue button </button>

sections.text: accepts any selector text. The value is trimmed of surrounding colons and then used both in the class name and in the generated selector.

sections.heading: Combining with a theme
sections.text: Because the theme is carried by the root builder, the same pseudo action can be used inside . The resulting class name reads from left to right: theme first, then the pseudo. Theme aware button Styles only inside a state The builder passed to , and intentionally exposes utilities but no nested states. Combine a pseudo with a responsive or theme variant from the outside instead.
sections.code: Dark Dark .Background(Color.Slate800) .Hover(h => h.Background(Color.Slate700)); // class names: // theme-dark:bg-slate-800 // theme-dark:hover:bg-slate-700 <button class="@Css.Px(6).Py(3).RoundedMd().FontBold().CursorPointer() @Css.Background(Color.Slate200).Color(Color.Slate800) @Css.Hover(h => h.Background(Color.Slate300)) @Dark.Background(Color.Slate800).Color(Color.Slate100) @Dark.Hover(h => h.Background(Color.Slate700))"> Theme aware button </button> Hover Focus Active

sections.text: Wrap utilities in a media query builder. FluentCss prefixes the class names so the browser can apply them conditionally.

sections.text: The method accepts any media query and a short prefix used to build the class name. This is how you add the breakpoints your design needs. sections.heading: Dark mode and themes
sections.text: A theme is an ancestor class. Build theme-aware styles with the Dark root, or create your own with Theme(name).

sections.heading: The Dark root
sections.text: is a shortcut for . It prefixes every utility in the chain with .
sections.code: Dark Theme("dark") theme-dark: Dark .Background(Color.Slate800) .Color(Color.Slate100) .Hover(h => h.Background(Color.Slate700)); // classes: // theme-dark:bg-slate-800 // theme-dark:text-slate-100 // theme-dark:hover:bg-slate-700

sections.heading: How the selector is built
sections.text: A themed utility is scoped by an ancestor that carries the theme class. The generated selector has two parts: the theme scope and the escaped utility class. Theme class goes on an ancestor Because the selector is a descendant combinator, the element that carries must be an ancestor of the styled element. Put it on or a wrapper element, not on the same element that also uses the utilities.
sections.code: /* .theme-dark is the ancestor, the theme class is escaped */ .theme-dark .theme-dark\:bg-slate-800 { background-color: oklch(0.279 0.041 260.031) } .theme-dark .theme-dark\:text-slate-100 { color: oklch(0.968 0.007 247.896) } theme-dark <html> @Dark

sections.heading: Toggling the theme
sections.text: Toggling is plain DOM work: add or remove the theme class. This documentation site persists the choice in a cookie and reads it on the server, so the theme class is part of the rendered element and the page never flashes the light theme first. is kept as a fallback for first visits. This card follows the theme. Use the toggle in the header to switch between light and dark.
sections.code:
localStorage // Read the saved choice. The server reads the same cookie to render the // theme class on , so this only handles the first visit. var theme = readCookie('fluentcss-theme') || localStorage.getItem('fluentcss-theme'); if (theme !== 'dark' && theme !== 'light') { theme = matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)').matches ? 'dark' : 'light'; } document.documentElement.classList.toggle('theme-dark', theme === 'dark'); // Toggle it somewhere (for example a button) and persist the choice. function fcToggleTheme() { var dark = document.documentElement.classList.toggle('theme-dark'); document.cookie = 'fluentcss-theme=' + (dark ? 'dark' : 'light') + ';path=/;max-age=31536000;samesite=lax'; }
This card follows the theme.
